patterns.signal: Deploys drop in-flight requests, or the orchestrator has to SIGKILL the service after the grace period
patterns.why: Catch SIGTERM, stop accepting work, drain in-flight requests, flush and close, then exit. Keep the drain shorter than the grace period, because SIGKILL cannot be caught.

patterns.signal: A service runs for hours, then fails with `Too many open files` while CPU and memory look normal
patterns.why: Close files, sockets and pipes on every path with `try/finally`, `using` or `with`. Descriptors are a per-process limit; raising `ulimit` only delays a leak.

patterns.signal: One misbehaving worker or plugin must not crash or corrupt the others
patterns.why: Processes get isolated memory, so a crash stays contained and the OS reclaims its resources. You pay in memory and IPC cost, since data must be copied or shared explicitly.

patterns.signal: Tasks need to share a large in-memory data set and hand work to each other cheaply
patterns.why: Threads share the address space, so no copying or IPC. Every shared mutable value now needs synchronization, and one thread's crash takes down the whole process.

patterns.signal: Two threads update a shared counter without a lock and the total is sometimes too low
patterns.why: `count++` is read-modify-write; interleaved threads lose updates. A mutex or atomic increment makes it indivisible. Keep critical sections short to limit contention.

patterns.signal: A profile or `strace` shows millions of tiny `read`/`write` syscalls and the I/O loop is slow
patterns.why: Each syscall crosses into the kernel and costs far more than a function call. A buffer turns many small calls into few large ones. Flush explicitly where durability or latency matters.

patterns.signal: A producer outpaces its consumer and memory grows steadily in an in-process queue
patterns.why: A bounded queue blocks, slows or rejects the producer when full, so overload becomes visible instead of an eventual OOM. You must choose: block, drop or shed with an error.

patterns.signal: Thread-per-connection server runs out of memory with thousands of mostly idle connections
patterns.why: One thread multiplexes many sockets via `epoll`/`kqueue`, so idle connections cost almost nothing. CPU-heavy or blocking calls on the loop stall everyone; offload them to a worker pool.

patterns.signal: URLs, ports and feature flags are hardcoded and differ between staging and production builds
patterns.why: Same artifact, different config per environment. Values are inherited strings read at start, so parse and validate them on boot and fail fast; changes need a restart.

patterns.signal: Each outgoing request opens a new connection and traces show DNS, TCP and TLS handshakes dominating latency
patterns.why: Reusing warm connections skips several round trips per call. Cap the pool size, and set idle timeouts below the server's so you never reuse a socket the peer already closed.

patterns.signal: A client sends hundreds of tiny messages per second, each as its own request or packet
patterns.why: Fixed per-message overhead (headers, round trips, syscalls) is paid once per batch. Flush on size or a short timer so batching never adds unbounded latency.

patterns.signal: Game state is sent 60 times per second and a late update is useless because a newer one follows
patterns.why: TCP would stall fresh data behind a retransmitted stale packet. Over UDP, tag messages with a sequence number and drop older ones; add your own reliability only for events that need it.

patterns.signal: A real-time TCP stream has small writes that arrive in bursts with roughly 40 ms extra delay
patterns.why: Nagle's algorithm holds small segments until the previous one is ACKed, which combines badly with delayed ACKs. Disabling it cuts latency but sends more packets, so batch writes yourself.

patterns.signal: A DNS record was changed but some clients keep reaching the old server for an hour
patterns.why: Resolvers cache records for the TTL, so drop it to minutes a full TTL before the change and keep the old server serving until traffic drains. Low TTLs mean more lookups.

patterns.signal: A client fails with a certificate error and someone proposes `verify=False` to make it work
patterns.use: Fix the trust chain, keep verification
patterns.why: Without verification TLS still encrypts but no longer proves who you talk to, so any man-in-the-middle wins. Install the missing CA or intermediate, or fix the hostname instead.

patterns.signal: A connection fails and you must decide where to look: refused immediately vs hangs until timeout
patterns.why: Refused means the host answered but nothing listens on that port. A hang usually means a firewall drops packets or the host is unreachable. Each points to a different layer.

patterns.signal: A server in a container listens on `127.0.0.1` and port-mapped requests from the host fail
patterns.why: Loopback inside the container is not the host's loopback, so forwarded traffic never reaches it. Bind all interfaces there and restrict exposure with the port mapping or a firewall.

patterns.signal: Users far from the data centre see slow page loads even though server processing time is small
patterns.why: A page load costs several round trips; terminating TCP and TLS at a nearby edge and caching static assets there shortens each one. Dynamic, per-user responses gain less.

patterns.signal: A client times out on `POST /payments` and retrying might charge the customer twice
patterns.why: The client sends a unique key per logical operation; the server stores the result under it and replays it on retry. Keys need a retention window and must be scoped to the caller.

patterns.signal: An infinite feed paged with `offset` shows duplicates or skips while new rows are inserted
patterns.why: Return an opaque cursor encoding the last sort key and query `WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor`. Stable under inserts and fast on deep pages, but no jumping to page N.

patterns.signal: One client sends thousands of requests per second and degrades the API for everyone else
patterns.why: A per-client token bucket protects shared capacity and `429` tells the client to slow down, unlike a `5xx`. Limits need a fair key (API key, user), not just IP.

patterns.signal: After an outage, every client retries at the same instant and knocks the recovering service over again
patterns.why: Doubling the delay spreads load over time and random jitter breaks synchronized waves. Cap the delay and attempt count, and only retry idempotent work or retryable statuses.

patterns.signal: A response field must be renamed or removed while old mobile app versions stay in the wild for months
patterns.why: Prefer additive changes; when breaking is unavoidable, publish `/v2` or a version header and run both until old clients fade. Every live version is code you must keep maintaining.

patterns.signal: Errors come back as `200 OK` with `{"error": ...}` and clients retry bad requests forever
patterns.why: `4xx` says fix the request, `5xx` says the server failed and a retry may help; `401` vs `403` separates identity from permission. Proxies, caches and retry logic depend on them.

patterns.signal: Clients re-download the same large, rarely changing resource on every request
patterns.why: The server returns an `ETag`; the client sends `If-None-Match` and gets a body-less `304 Not Modified` when nothing changed. Saves bandwidth, but still costs one round trip.

patterns.signal: A report or export request takes minutes and HTTP calls hit gateway timeouts
patterns.why: Accept the job, return a URL to poll or a callback, and run it in the background. Turns a fragile long request into a tracked job, at the cost of extra state and polling.

patterns.signal: A mobile screen makes five sequential calls and discards most of each response
patterns.why: One request shaped to the screen cuts round trips and overfetch. GraphQL loses easy HTTP caching and needs query cost limits; a BFF is simpler but tied to one client.

patterns.signal: Browsers poll an endpoint every second to learn about rare server-side changes
patterns.why: Push over one long-lived connection gives lower latency and far fewer empty responses. SSE is one-way over plain HTTP; WebSocket is two-way. Both need reconnect and resume logic.

patterns.signal: `WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20` is slow on a large table
patterns.use: Composite index: filter column, then sort
patterns.why: An index on `(customer_id, created_at)` finds the rows and returns them pre-sorted, so the database stops after 20. Column order matters; each index slows writes.

patterns.signal: An index was added but the endpoint is still slow and nobody checked what the database actually does
patterns.why: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows sequential scans, unused indexes, bad row estimates and sorts. Measure on production-sized data; a tiny dev table can make any plan look fine.

patterns.signal: Logs show one list query followed by hundreds of near-identical `SELECT ... WHERE id = ?`
patterns.why: Fetch related rows in one `JOIN` or one `WHERE id IN (...)` batch instead of a query per row. ORMs hide this behind lazy loading; enable eager loading for that access path.

patterns.signal: Code reads a balance, subtracts in the app, writes it back, and concurrent requests lose updates
patterns.why: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 30` does read and write in one step. Check affected rows to detect the failed condition.

patterns.signal: Two users edit the same record over minutes and the later save silently overwrites the earlier one
patterns.use: Optimistic locking with a version column
patterns.why: Write with `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` and bump the version; zero affected rows means conflict, so reload and retry or ask the user. Wins at low contention, thrashes at high.

patterns.signal: Several writes must all happen or none, such as debit one account and credit another
patterns.why: Atomicity rolls back a partial failure. Isolation level decides which anomalies remain, so pick it deliberately. Keep transactions short and never wait on network calls inside one.

patterns.signal: Duplicate emails appear despite a `SELECT` check in application code before insert
patterns.why: A check-then-insert races between requests; only the database can enforce uniqueness atomically. Catch the constraint violation and map it to a clean `409` for the client.

patterns.signal: The same customer address is copied into many rows and updates leave some copies stale
patterns.use: Normalise to one fact, one place
patterns.why: Store it once and reference it by foreign key so updates cannot diverge. Denormalise later only for a measured read hotspot, and own the work of keeping copies in sync.

patterns.signal: The primary's CPU is saturated by reporting and read traffic while writes are a small share
patterns.why: Route heavy reads to followers to offload the primary. Async replicas lag, so a read right after a write can be stale; keep read-after-write paths on the primary.

patterns.signal: A team wants to move a plain relational app to NoSQL 'because it scales' with no measured bottleneck
patterns.use: Stay relational until a measured need
patterns.why: Relational databases scale far with indexes, replicas and caching while keeping joins, constraints and transactions. Choose a document or key-value store for a specific access pattern.

patterns.signal: A remote call has no timeout, or code treats a read timeout as a definite failure
patterns.why: Every remote call needs a deadline. A timeout means the work may or may not have happened, so retry with the same idempotency key or query the status before acting again.

patterns.signal: A downstream dependency is down and request threads pile up waiting on it until the caller dies too
patterns.why: After repeated failures the breaker opens and fails fast, then lets trial calls through to probe recovery. Stops cascades, but you need a fallback and well-tuned thresholds.

patterns.signal: A queue consumer sends duplicate welcome emails after crashes and redeliveries
patterns.why: At-least-once delivery guarantees duplicates eventually. Record processed message ids (or use a natural key) in the same transaction as the side effect and skip repeats.

patterns.signal: Code writes to the database, then publishes an event, and a crash in between loses or fakes the event
patterns.why: Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the state change; a relay publishes it afterwards. Gives at-least-once publishing, so consumers must still dedupe.

patterns.signal: One business operation spans several services' databases and no distributed transaction is available
patterns.why: Run local transactions step by step and on failure run compensations (refund, release stock) in reverse. Intermediate states are visible, and compensations must be idempotent.

patterns.signal: A scheduled job runs on every replica and should run on exactly one
patterns.why: Replicas compete for an expiring lease in a coordinator (etcd, ZooKeeper, a DB row). A paused old leader may still act, so protect writes with a fencing token.

patterns.signal: A read-heavy lookup hits the database every time and can tolerate a few seconds of staleness
patterns.why: Read the cache, on miss load from the DB and populate it; on write, invalidate the key. Simple and only caches what is used, but the first read is slow and staleness is bounded only by TTL.

patterns.signal: Reads right after a write must see the new value and the cache sits in front of every read
patterns.why: Writes update the cache and the store together, so cached reads are fresh. Write latency rises, and you cache data that may never be read; pair with TTLs to evict it.

patterns.signal: A hot cache key expires and thousands of identical queries hit the database at once
patterns.why: Let one request recompute while others wait or serve the stale value (single-flight, a lock, early refresh), and jitter TTLs so keys do not expire together. Adds complexity to the cache path.

patterns.signal: Keys are spread over cache nodes with `hash(key) % N` and adding one node invalidates almost everything
patterns.why: Nodes sit on a hash ring and only about 1/N of keys move when one is added or removed. Use virtual nodes to even out the load; hot single keys still need separate handling.

patterns.signal: A user saves their profile, is redirected, and sees old data because reads go to an async follower
patterns.why: Route that user's reads to the leader for a short window, or until the follower has caught up to their write position. Costs leader load and session-aware routing.

patterns.signal: A design requires strong consistency and full availability even during network partitions
patterns.why: During a partition you must refuse some requests or serve possibly stale data; even when healthy, stronger consistency costs latency. Decide per operation: balances vs like counts.

patterns.signal: SQL is built by concatenating or formatting user input into the query string
patterns.why: Placeholders send data separately from the SQL text, so input can never become code. Identifiers such as column names cannot be parameters; pick those from an allowlist.

patterns.signal: A shell command string is assembled with a filename or argument that comes from a user
patterns.why: Pass an argv array to the process API with shell execution off, so `;` or `$()` stay literal. Still validate the values, and reject leading `-` that could become an option.

patterns.signal: User-supplied text is inserted into HTML, attributes or inline scripts
patterns.why: Escape for the exact context at render time, ideally via an auto-escaping template engine. Raw-HTML escape hatches bypass it; add a Content Security Policy as a second layer.

patterns.signal: `GET /api/invoices/1042` returns any invoice to any logged-in user who changes the id
patterns.why: Authentication proves who the caller is; every request must also check server-side that this caller may access this specific record. Unguessable ids help but are not access control.

patterns.signal: An API key or password was committed to a repository, even if removed in the next commit
patterns.use: Revoke and rotate the leaked secret
patterns.why: Git history, forks and scanners keep it forever, and bots find public keys in minutes. Revoke and issue a new one first, then check logs for misuse; history rewriting is optional cleanup.

patterns.signal: Credentials live in source files, config committed to git, or are shared over chat
patterns.why: Store secrets in a vault or the platform's secret store and inject them at runtime, with access control, audit logs and rotation. Keep them out of logs and error messages too.

patterns.signal: A read-only report job connects to the database as the owner account
patterns.why: A dedicated role with `SELECT` on just the needed tables limits the blast radius if the job is compromised or buggy. Costs some setup and occasional permission requests.

patterns.signal: Passwords are stored with a fast hash like SHA-256 or MD5, or unsalted
patterns.why: Use Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt with a per-user salt so offline guessing is expensive. Tune the cost to tens of milliseconds per login; never encrypt passwords reversibly.

patterns.signal: A new feature handles payments, uploads or admin actions and nobody has asked what could go wrong
patterns.why: List assets, trust boundaries, plausible attackers and impact before building, then put controls where input crosses a boundary. A short whiteboard session beats auditing afterwards.

patterns.signal: A single control, such as the firewall or the login page, is the only thing protecting sensitive data
patterns.why: Layer independent controls (authz checks, encryption, network rules, monitoring) so one mistake is not a breach. Each layer adds cost, so prioritise by asset value from the threat model.
